title: Optik Art earrings
lede: A pair of square earrings in white acrylic, screen-printed with nested black squares and rings, from Wendy Ramshaw and David Watkins’s Optik Art Jewellery.
summary: White perspex squares turned on point and printed with concentric black squares and circles. Ramshaw and Watkins, London, 1963–65.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A photograph of the pair T.338E&F-1982 (1600 × 1308 px), on black, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Black and white op geometry at the smallest scale: rings and squares nested so that figure and ground swap. Partial fit: a single motif, not an all-over field.

context: The V&A describes the pair as screen-printed acrylic (perspex) and base metal: an opaque white square with a screen-printed black op-art design. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1194608/).

The V&A’s record of a related ring says that Ramshaw and Watkins began Optik Art Jewellery in 1963, “inspired by Op-Art”. They screen-printed black and white patterns onto acrylic sheets and sliced the sheets into pieces, and Fenwicks of Bond Street commissioned collections. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O145843/).
observed: Each earring is a flat square turned 45 degrees, with a black ground.
Inside, a white ring holds a black square on point, which holds a smaller white ring and a black square: circles and squares alternate inward.
Where a circle crosses a square, the white areas split into crescents and triangles, so figure and ground alternate.
The edges of the acrylic show as thin white lines.
interpretation: The earrings reduce op art to one emblem, much like Vasarely’s square-in-circle units, and make it a cheap fashion product.
Screen printing on a sheet and cutting it into pieces is the same industrial logic that made op prints easy to reproduce.
borrow: Nest alternating circles and squares in black and white so that the crossings make crescents and triangles.
Turn a square badge or icon 45 degrees to give a static motif tension.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The designs are in copyright, and the V&A photograph is not openly licensed.
